chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the Fitra (alms-tax on the head), how much should be paid on behalf of every head from wheat, barley, dates, and raisins? He said: A Sa'a, by the Sa'a of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family).

key_terms.التَّمْر: Dates: A common staple in the Arabian peninsula, included in the Fitra calculation.
key_terms.الزَّبِيب: Raisins: Dried grapes, also included as a valid form of payment for Fitra.
key_terms.الشَّعِير: Barley: Another staple food subject to the Fitra ruling.
key_terms.النَّبِيّ: The Prophet: Referring to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family), whose standard of measurement is the reference.
key_terms.الْحِنْطَة: Wheat: One of the primary staple foods for which the Fitra measure is calculated.
key_terms.الْفِطْرَة: Fitra: A specific obligatory alms-tax or head tax in Shia fiqh, distinct from Zakat al-Fitr in some contexts, often paid on the head of the family for dependents.
key_terms.صَاعٌ: Sa'a: A traditional unit of volume measure used for determining the quantity of Zakat and Fitra.

ai.seo_question: What is the prescribed amount and measure for Fitra in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the Fitra obligation is fixed at one Sa'a per head, explicitly linking the measurement to the Prophet's standard to ensure consistency in Islamic jurisprudence. This narration underscores the practical application of Zakat as a means of spiritual purification and social welfare, emphasizing the importance of adhering to traditional volumetric measures for staple foods like wheat, barley, dates, and raisins. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the continuity of prophetic practice in determining obligatory dues.
